claims.claim: Power is the capacity to influence others; management texts define it as the ability to influence others to behave in a particular way, and the French and Raven tradition defines social power as the potential for such influence.

The five classic bases of power — legitimate, reward, coercive, expert, and referent — originate in the 1959 study by social psychologists John French and Bertram Raven (some texts cite 1960), and remain the standard framework for talking about influence in organizations.

Legitimate power derives from an individual's organizational role or position; reward power from control over things others value; coercive power from the ability to threaten negative outcomes; expert power from extensive knowledge others trust; referent power from personal charisma and the respect or admiration the person inspires.

The bases group into position power (legitimate, reward, coercive — attached to the role) and personal power (expert, referent — attached to the person); management texts contrast managers' position-derived power with leaders' power from followers' perceptions of their expertise, personality, and relationships.

Influence tactics are specific actions used to carry influence in a given situation; the standard tactic set includes rational persuasion (facts, data, and logic — the most commonly applied tactic), consultation (asking others to help shape the plan), coalition tactics (a group working together toward a common goal), and exchange (trading something of value for compliance).

Having power and using power are different things: a manager who can reward or punish is usually obeyed even when no reward or punishment is actually given, because the mere capacity produces compliance.

Power is follower-dependent and attributed: followers accept or reject acts of leadership and can surrender or withhold their power, so influence works only while the people being influenced keep granting it.

Leadership is at bottom a social (interpersonal) influence relationship, which is why power and influence are central to leading; this lesson references leading, ethics, and leadership styles only as sibling topics.

positions: The classic French and Raven (1959) framework lists five bases: coercive, reward, legitimate, referent, expert.
Raven later added informational power (1965), and some texts (e.g., University of Minnesota Organizational Behavior 13.3) present six sources of power.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the canonical five bases named in the subject source map, with one passing remark that some later treatments add a sixth base (informational power); all questions and examples use the five.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Citation year for the French and Raven study
positions: University of Minnesota Organizational Behavior cites 1960.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the framework to the French and Raven tradition and calls it 'a classic study,' avoiding a specific year; the evidence notes record both dates honestly.

positions: OpenStax Introduction to Business defines power as the ability to influence others to behave in a particular way.
French and Raven define social power as the potential for influence (the ability of an agent to bring about change in another person).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses 'the capacity to influence others' as its working definition, which both formulations support, and attributes the definition to the management tradition.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The phase-2 machine-generated draft ('Power And Influence is a foundational concept in Management & Leadership...') contained only generic boilerplate and no factual claims; it was discarded in full and replaced with source-verified content.
correctionsNeeded: Rewrote the boilerplate draft entirely from verified sources; no draft wording was retained.
Attributed the five-bases framework to the French and Raven tradition rather than presenting it as unattributed general knowledge.

Replaced the draft's vague framing with the lesson's explicit scope: definition, five bases, position vs personal power, four named influence tactics, honest ethics note, and the borrowed-power framing.
All examples were written as original scenarios (bakery supervisor, clinic physician, library clerks, project team, Rina the baker); none were taken from any source.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, Section 6.4: Leading, Guiding, and Motivating Others
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Wayback Machine capture of the canonical OpenStax URL (web.archive.org/web/2023/...). Supports the working definition of power ('the ability to influence others to behave in a particular way') and one-line descriptions of the five bases (legitimate from position, reward from control over rewards, coercive from the ability to threaten negative outcomes, expert from extensive knowledge, referent from personal charisma and the respect/admiration inspired). Facts restated in original prose; CC BY 4.0 text not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Management, Section 13.1: The Nature of Leadership
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Wayback Machine capture of the canonical OpenStax URL (web.archive.org/web/2023/...). Supports the position-versus-personal contrast ('managers commonly derive power from the position they occupy... leaders derive power from followers' perception of their knowledge (expertise), their personality and attractiveness, and the working relationship'), leadership as a social influence relationship, and the notion that leadership depends on followers' acceptance or rejection. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Management, Section 13.2: The Leadership Process
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Wayback Machine capture of the canonical OpenStax URL (web.archive.org/web/2023/...). Supports the follower-dependence of power: it is the follower who either rejects leadership or accepts acts of leadership by surrendering his power to the leader. Used as the basis for the lesson's honest framing that power is borrowed from followers. Facts restated in original prose.

Facts restated in original prose; OER text not reproduced.
